lessons.title: Why We Have Laws
body: Imagine a game with no rules. Everyone would argue about who won, and the strongest or loudest player would get their way. A society without laws would have the same problem on a much bigger scale. Laws are rules that a government makes and enforces. They have a few main jobs.

First, laws protect people and property. Rules against assault and theft keep you safe and let you keep what you own. Second, laws settle disputes in a peaceful way. If two neighbors disagree about a fence, a court can decide instead of the neighbors fighting. Third, laws set up how the government itself works, such as who can make rules and how leaders are chosen. Fourth, laws protect freedoms, so that even a powerful official cannot take away your basic rights without a fair process.

A key idea is the rule of law. It means the same rules apply to everyone, including leaders, and that rules must be written down and known ahead of time. A rule that changes in secret, or that applies only to some people, is not the rule of law.

Laws are different from morals and manners. Lying to a friend may be wrong, but it is usually not illegal. Chewing with your mouth open is rude, but no police officer will arrest you for it. Some things are both wrong and illegal, like stealing. People can disagree about what laws should say, and that is why we have ways to change them.

lessons.title: Four Sources of Law
body: In the United States, law comes from four main places, and they fit together like layers.

The first is a constitution. The United States Constitution is the highest law in the country. It sets up the government and limits what the government may do. Each state also has its own constitution.
The second is a statute. A statute is a law passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature. A rule that says you must wear a seat belt is usually a statute.

The third is a regulation. Legislatures often create agencies, like the Food and Drug Administration, and give them power to write detailed rules. These rules are called regulations. They carry the force of law, but they must stay within what the statute allows.

The fourth is case law, also called common law. When judges decide cases, they explain the reasons for their decision. Later courts usually follow those earlier decisions. This habit of following earlier decisions is called precedent. It helps similar cases come out the same way.

When two sources clash, the higher one wins. A statute that goes against the Constitution can be struck down by a court. A regulation that goes beyond its statute can also be challenged. A good way to remember it is that the Constitution is the top shelf, and everything else has to fit under it.

lessons.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
body: A bill is a proposed law. Under the United States Constitution, a federal bill follows a set path through Congress. Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and both must agree on the same text.

A member of Congress introduces a bill. It goes to a committee, a small group that studies the topic, may hold hearings, and can change the bill. If the committee approves it, the full chamber debates and votes. A simple majority is usually enough to pass.
Then the bill goes to the other chamber, which goes through the same steps. If the two chambers pass different versions, they must work out the differences and both vote on the final text.

Next the bill goes to the President. The President can sign it, which makes it law. The President can also veto it, which sends it back to Congress. Congress can override a veto if two thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to pass it again. If the President does nothing for ten days, not counting Sundays, while Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature.

Most bills never become law. Many die in committee. This long path is on purpose. It gives many people a chance to improve a bill or stop a bad one. States use similar steps, and city councils pass local laws called ordinances.

lessons.title: Local, State and Federal Law
body: The United States shares power between a national government and the fifty state governments. This is called federalism. Cities and counties add a third level.

The federal government handles things that affect the whole country, such as national defense, immigration, coining money, and trade between states. States handle many everyday matters, including most criminal law, schools, driver licenses, and marriage rules. Cities and counties make local rules about things like parking, zoning, and noise.

This means the law can be different depending on where you are. The age at which you can get a driver license, the speed limit on a road, and the rules for a school day all vary by state or town. If you move, you may need to learn new rules.

Sometimes levels overlap. Some actions can break both a state and a federal law. When a federal law and a state law truly conflict, the Constitution says federal law wins, as long as the federal law is within the powers the Constitution gives to the national government. This is called the Supremacy Clause.

For example, a city may set a curfew for young people, while the state sets the minimum age for working. A federal law then sets national rules for things like child labor in many jobs. All three can apply to you at once.

lessons.title: Civil Versus Criminal
body: Courts hear two big kinds of cases. In a criminal case, the government says that a person broke a law that protects the whole community, such as a law against theft. The government is called the prosecution. The person accused is the defendant. If the defendant is found guilty, the punishment can include fines, probation, or time in jail or prison.

In a civil case, one person or group sues another, usually over money or a right. The one who sues is the plaintiff, and the other is the defendant. Suppose a neighbor's tree falls on your garage because the neighbor ignored a warning. You might file a civil case asking the court to order the neighbor to pay for repairs. A civil case does not send anyone to jail for the underlying dispute. The usual result is money damages or a court order.

The standard of proof is also different. In a criminal case, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, which is a very high bar. In most civil cases, the plaintiff only needs to show that their side is more likely true than not, called a preponderance of the evidence.

One event can lead to both kinds of cases. If a driver hits a pedestrian while breaking traffic laws, the state may bring a criminal case, and the pedestrian may bring a separate civil case for medical bills.

lessons.title: Judges, Juries and Fair Trials
body: A fair trial is one of the most important protections in a free country. The Constitution promises due process, which means the government must follow fair steps before it takes away someone's life, liberty, or property.

In a trial, the judge acts like a referee. The judge decides what rules apply, decides what evidence the jury may hear, and keeps order. The jury is a group of ordinary citizens who listen to the evidence and decide what the facts are. In a criminal case, the jury decides whether the defendant is guilty or not guilty. A judge alone can also decide a case when there is no jury, and that is called a bench trial.

The lawyers play different roles. The prosecutor presents the government's case. The defense lawyer speaks for the defendant. Each side can question witnesses and make arguments. Witnesses swear to tell the truth.

The Constitution gives people accused of crimes several key protections. They are presumed innocent until proven guilty. They have the right to a lawyer, and if they cannot afford one, the government must provide one in serious cases. They have the right to remain silent. They have the right to confront the witnesses against them.
These rules exist because mistakes can be very costly. It is better to have a careful process that protects the innocent, even if it also means some rules must be followed strictly by everyone.

lessons.title: Juvenile Justice
body: Most states have a separate court system for young people, called the juvenile justice system. It began more than a hundred years ago with the idea that young people are still growing and can often change, so the goal should be to guide them, not just punish them.

In juvenile court, the language is different. A young person is usually said to be adjudicated delinquent rather than convicted. The hearing is often private to protect the young person. Results may include probation, counseling, community service, or time in a youth facility. The details vary a great deal from state to state, including the age at which a person is treated as a juvenile.

For many years, juvenile courts were informal, and young people often had few legal protections. In 1967, in a case called In re Gault, the United States Supreme Court said that young people in delinquency cases facing possible loss of freedom have important due process rights. These include the right to a lawyer, notice of the charges, and the right to question witnesses.

In serious cases, some states allow or require a young person to be tried in adult court. People disagree about when this should happen. Some argue it protects the public. Others argue that young people have more capacity to change. States make their own choices within limits set by the Constitution.
If you or a friend ever have questions about a real situation, the best step is to talk to a trusted adult and a licensed lawyer.

lessons.title: Talking With Police and Your Rights
body: The Fifth Amendment says that no one can be forced to be a witness against themselves. This is the right to remain silent. It protects you from being pressured into saying things that could be used against you.

In 1966, in Miranda v. Arizona, the Supreme Court held that before police question a person who is in custody, they must warn the person of key rights. Those rights include the right to stay silent, the warning that anything said can be used in court, the right to a lawyer, and the right to have a lawyer appointed if the person cannot afford one. People often call these the Miranda warnings. They are required when someone is both in custody and being questioned. Police do not have to read them every time they talk to someone.

In 2011, in J.D.B. v. North Carolina, the Court said that a child's age can matter when deciding whether a young person felt free to leave during police questioning at school. Children may feel more pressure than adults.

What should a young person do? Staying calm and polite matters. You can say clearly that you want to talk with a parent or guardian and a lawyer before answering questions. You should never lie, run, or fight. Having a trusted adult present is a smart protection. This is general education and not legal advice, and real situations call for a real lawyer.

lessons.title: Contracts: Promises the Law Enforces
body: A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. You make small contracts all the time. When you buy a snack, you agree to pay and the store agrees to give you the snack.

Most contracts need a few parts. First is an offer, where one side proposes a deal. Second is acceptance, where the other side agrees to those terms. Third is consideration, which means each side gives or promises something of value, like money for goods. Both sides must also intend to be bound, and the deal must be for something legal. A promise to sell stolen goods is not an enforceable contract.

Contracts do not always have to be written. Many spoken agreements count. But some important ones, such as the sale of land, must be in writing to be enforced. A written contract is also much easier to prove.

Minors have special protection. In general, a contract made by someone under eighteen is voidable, which means the minor may choose to cancel it. The other side usually cannot cancel just because the minor can. There are exceptions, such as for necessities like food and clothing, and the rules differ by state. Because of this, stores and companies often ask a parent or guardian to sign for a young person.
Before agreeing to anything, read the terms, ask questions, and never sign something you do not understand.

lessons.title: Being a Smart Consumer
body: A consumer is someone who buys goods or services for personal use. Laws protect consumers from being tricked or sold dangerous products.

A warranty is a promise about a product. Some warranties are written, such as a company promising to fix a phone for one year. Others are implied, which means the law reads them in even if nobody said them. For goods sold by a merchant, the law generally implies that the product is fit for ordinary use. Sellers can sometimes limit these promises, but only if they follow rules about how they say so.

Refunds are not always required by law. Many stores have their own return policies, so it helps to check them before buying. Some states and some types of sales have special rules, like cooling off periods for certain door-to-door sales.
False advertising is unlawful. The Federal Trade Commission, or FTC, enforces rules against deceptive or unfair business practices. States have their own consumer protection offices.

Scams are common, especially online. Warning signs include pressure to act right now, requests to pay with gift cards or wire transfers, offers that seem too good to be true, and messages asking for passwords. Real companies do not ask for your password by text.
If you have a problem, keep records such as receipts and screenshots, contact the seller first, and then ask a parent or guardian to help you reach a consumer protection office.

lessons.title: Property: Yours, Mine and Borrowed
body: Property is anything a person can own. The law divides it into two main kinds. Real property is land and things permanently attached to it, like a house. Personal property is everything else that can be moved, such as a bike, a phone, or a guitar.

Owning something comes with rights. The owner can use it, sell it, give it away, and generally keep others from using it. But rights have limits. You cannot use your property in a way that seriously harms others, such as playing extremely loud music all night.

When someone enters land without permission, it is called trespass. Even if the land is empty, posted signs or fences can show that entry is not allowed. Taking someone else's personal property without permission, with the intent to keep it, is theft. Borrowing is different from taking, but only if the owner agrees. If you borrow a friend's game and break it, the friend may expect you to pay for the damage.

Renting is a middle path. A tenant pays rent to use a home that a landlord owns. A lease is the contract that sets the rules, such as how long the rental lasts and who fixes what. Both sides have duties. The tenant should pay rent and not damage the home. The landlord generally must keep the home safe to live in.
Found items also raise questions. If you find a wallet, the right thing to do is to try to return it or turn it in. Laws about found property vary by place.

lessons.title: Privacy Online
body: Every time you use an app or website, information about you may be collected. This can include your name, location, what you search for, and what you click. Companies use this data to improve services, to show ads, and sometimes to sell to other businesses. Privacy law is about how this information may be collected and used.

In the United States, there is no single law covering all privacy. Instead there are many laws for different areas. One important law for young people is the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, called COPPA. It applies to websites and apps directed at children under thirteen, and to other sites that know a user is under thirteen. These services generally must get a parent's permission before collecting personal information. This is one reason many services say you must be thirteen or older to sign up.
Terms of service and privacy policies are agreements you accept when you sign up. They explain what the company will do with your data. Most people never read them, but they matter.

You can protect yourself. Use strong, different passwords. Do not share your address, school, or phone number publicly. Review privacy settings. Remember that anything you post can be copied or screenshot, even if you delete it. Think about whether you would be comfortable if a parent, a teacher, or a future employer saw it.
If something feels wrong, tell a trusted adult.

lessons.title: Copyright, Sharing and Remixing
body: Copyright is a legal right that protects original creative work, such as songs, books, photos, videos, drawings, and software. In the United States, protection starts automatically the moment the work is created and fixed in some form. The creator does not have to file a form or add a copyright symbol, although registration offers extra benefits.

Copyright gives the owner the exclusive right to do certain things, like copy the work, share it, and make new versions based on it. If you do these things with someone else's work without permission, you may be infringing. That is true even if you give credit. Giving credit is polite and avoids plagiarism, but it does not by itself make copying legal.

Copyright does not last forever, and it does not protect everything. Ideas and facts are not protected, only the way they are expressed. Works whose copyright has expired are in the public domain, and anyone can use them.

There is also a doctrine called fair use. Courts look at factors such as the purpose of the use, the type of work, how much was used, and the effect on the market for the original. Using a short quote in a school report is more likely to be fair than posting a whole movie. Fair use is decided case by case, so no simple percentage rule exists.
Creative Commons licenses let creators say ahead of time how others may use their work. Look for these licenses when you need images or music for a project.

lessons.title: Cyberbullying and the Law
body: Cyberbullying is bullying that happens through phones, games, apps, or social media. It can include sending cruel messages, spreading rumors, sharing embarrassing pictures, or leaving someone out on purpose to hurt them. Because it can reach someone at any hour and be seen by many people, it can feel especially painful.

There is no single national cyberbullying law. Instead, most states have laws that require schools to have anti-bullying policies, and some states specifically mention electronic harassment. Some states also have criminal laws that can apply to serious cases, such as harassment, stalking, threats, or sharing private images of a minor. The details vary widely.

Schools can sometimes act on online behavior, but there are limits. Courts have said students keep some free speech rights, so schools have to be careful when punishing speech that happens away from school. They usually have stronger reasons to act when the behavior seriously disrupts school or targets a student in a way that affects their education.
Sharing intimate images of anyone under eighteen can be a very serious crime, even when the people in the images are teens themselves. Never ask for, take, or pass along such images.

If you are targeted, you can save screenshots, block the person, and tell a trusted adult. If you see it happening to someone else, you can support the person and report it. Small actions by bystanders can make a big difference.

lessons.title: Your Rights at School
body: The Constitution applies in public schools, but students' rights there are not exactly the same as adults' rights in public. Courts try to balance students' rights with the school's job of keeping order and a safe place to learn.

On speech, the key case is Tinker v. Des Moines in 1969. Students wore black armbands to protest a war and were suspended. The Supreme Court said students do not shed their free speech rights at the schoolhouse gate. A school can limit student speech if it would materially and substantially disrupt school activities or invade the rights of others, but it cannot punish speech just because it dislikes the opinion. Later cases have given schools more power in some situations, such as lewd speech at an assembly. In 2021, in Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., the Court held that a school had gone too far when it punished a student for a crude off-campus social media post, though it did not say schools can never act on off-campus speech.

On searches, New Jersey v. T.L.O. in 1985 held that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials, but a school official needs only reasonable grounds for suspicion, not full probable cause, to search a student.
On discipline, students facing suspension generally have a right to notice and a chance to explain.
These rules mostly apply to public schools, and private schools often have different rules. Your school handbook explains the local policies.

lessons.title: What Is International Law?
body: International law is the set of rules that govern how countries deal with each other. Unlike the law inside a country, there is no world government that writes laws and no world police force. So where do the rules come from?

The most important source is the treaty. A treaty is a written agreement between countries. A country that joins a treaty is called a party. Treaties can be between two countries, like a trade agreement, or among many, like a treaty about the oceans. A basic principle is that countries must keep their treaty promises. Lawyers use the Latin phrase pacta sunt servanda for this. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, from 1969, sets out many of the rules about how treaties are made and interpreted.

The second major source is custom. Some rules are not written in any one treaty but are followed by countries consistently because they feel legally required to do so. For example, the idea that diplomats should not be harmed has a long history.
Countries also generally accept some general principles of fairness, and the writings of respected scholars and past court decisions help show what the rules are.
In the United States, a treaty is made by the President with the advice and consent of two thirds of the Senate, and ratified treaties are part of the supreme law of the land under the Constitution.

lessons.title: The United Nations
body: The United Nations, or UN, was created in 1945, right after the Second World War, with the goal of preventing future wars and helping countries work together. Its founding treaty is the Charter of the United Nations. Today almost every recognized country in the world is a member, with 193 member states.

The UN has several main parts. The General Assembly includes all members, each with one vote, and it discusses world issues and passes resolutions. Most of its resolutions are recommendations and are not legally binding on countries. The Security Council has fifteen members. Five are permanent members, which are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Each of these five can veto a major decision. The Security Council is the one body whose decisions can be binding on member states, and it can authorize actions such as sanctions or peacekeeping missions.

The International Court of Justice, often called the World Court, sits in The Hague in the Netherlands. It is the main judicial body of the UN. It settles disputes between countries and gives advice on legal questions when asked.

The Charter says that countries should settle disputes peacefully and should not use force against other countries, with limited exceptions such as self-defense and actions authorized by the Security Council.
People disagree about how well the UN works. Supporters say it prevents conflict and delivers aid. Critics point to the veto, which can block action.

lessons.title: Human Rights Across Borders
body: Human rights are basic protections that belong to every person simply because they are human, no matter where they live. After the terrible harms of the Second World War, countries wanted a shared statement of these rights.

In 1948, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, often called the UDHR. It lists rights such as life, liberty, equality before the law, freedom of thought and expression, and the right to education. When it was adopted, it was a declaration and not a binding treaty. Over time, many of its ideas have been written into binding treaties and have influenced national laws.

Two major treaties followed in 1966, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Other treaties focus on particular groups or harms, such as one against racial discrimination and one on women's rights.

For young people, the key treaty is the Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989. It says children have rights to things like education, health care, protection from harm, and having their views heard. Nearly every country has joined it. The United States signed it but has not ratified it, so it is not binding on the United States as a treaty.
Human rights treaties are only as strong as their enforcement. Some regions have courts, like the European Court of Human Rights, where people can bring complaints.

lessons.title: Why Countries Follow or Break Rules
body: If no world police can force a country to obey, why do countries follow international law most of the time? There are several reasons.

One is reciprocity. If one country breaks a trade agreement, the other can respond in kind. Countries want others to keep their promises, so they usually keep their own. Another is reputation. A country known for breaking its word will find it harder to make future deals. A third is self-interest. Rules about shipping, air travel, and mail work because everyone benefits from predictability. Finally, many countries bring international rules into their own laws, so their own courts and officials apply them.

Still, rules are sometimes broken. When this happens, there are tools. Countries can protest, bring a case to a court, or use diplomacy. They can also use countermeasures such as trade restrictions. The UN Security Council can impose sanctions, which are penalties like limits on trade or travel, though a veto can block action.

Courts have limits. The International Court of Justice can hear a dispute between countries only if they have agreed to its jurisdiction in some way. Its judgments are binding on the parties, but it has no police to carry them out. The International Criminal Court, set up by the Rome Statute, prosecutes individuals for the gravest crimes, but not every country is a member, and some governments dispute its authority.
So international law works less by force and more by shared interest, pressure, and habit.

questions.prompt: Which idea means that the same rules apply to everyone, including leaders, and that rules must be known ahead of time?
choices: The rule of law, which applies written and public rules equally to all people
The rule of majority, which lets the most popular group decide every issue
The rule of custom, which treats old habits as automatically binding law
The rule of the executive, which gives top officials final say over disputes

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of something that is wrong but usually not against the law?
choices: Taking a bicycle from a neighbor's garage without asking permission
Telling a friend a small lie about why you could not come over
Hitting a classmate on the playground during a disagreement
Selling a product that you know is dangerous to young children

questions.prompt: A town court decides which of two neighbors owns a disputed strip of land, and both accept the result. Which purpose of law is this best showing?
choices: Protecting freedoms by limiting what government officials may do
Setting up the structure of how government itself operates
Settling disputes between people in a peaceful and orderly way
Punishing wrongdoing so that other people are discouraged

questions.prompt: A city secretly changes a parking rule overnight and fines only residents of one street who had no way to learn of it. Which principle is most clearly violated?
choices: The idea that every violation must lead to a criminal trial
The idea that local governments cannot make any rules
The idea that all laws must come from a national legislature
The idea that rules must be public, known, and applied equally

questions.prompt: What is a regulation?
choices: A law passed directly by voters in a neighborhood election each year
A written opinion from a judge explaining how a case was decided
A part of the Constitution that explains how elections must be run
A detailed rule written by an agency under power given by a statute

questions.prompt: What is the name for the habit of courts following earlier decisions in similar cases?
choices: Veto
Ratification
Precedent
Ordinance

questions.prompt: A state statute conflicts with a clear rule in the United States Constitution. What is the likely result in court?
choices: The court must send the issue to a state agency to decide
The statute can be struck down because the Constitution ranks higher
The statute wins because state legislatures are closer to the people
The Constitution and statute both apply to the same extent

questions.prompt: Congress passes a statute allowing an agency to set safety standards for toys. The agency then issues a rule banning all outdoor play equipment, which the statute does not cover. Which challenge is strongest?
choices: The rule is invalid because it goes beyond what the statute authorized
The rule is invalid because agencies are never allowed to write rules
The rule is valid because agency rules always outrank statutes
The rule is valid because the agency can expand its own powers freely

questions.prompt: Which two bodies must both pass a federal bill in the same form?
choices: The House and the Supreme Court
The Supreme Court and the President
The House of Representatives and the Senate
The Senate and the Cabinet

questions.prompt: What majority does Congress need in each chamber to override a presidential veto?
choices: A unanimous vote from every single member
A simple majority of members present at the vote
Three fourths of the members in each chamber
Two thirds of the members in each chamber

questions.prompt: A bill passes the House but is changed by the Senate before passing there. What must happen before it goes to the President?
choices: Both chambers must agree on identical final text
The President must choose which version to approve
The Supreme Court must pick the version that is clearer
The House must give up and accept the Senate version

questions.prompt: A member of Congress says, "If a bill is stuck in committee, it will still become law if the President likes it." What is wrong with this claim?
choices: Committees only hold bills for a few days and then must release them
A bill must pass the full chamber, and a committee can stop it first
A bill requires a signature from every state governor beforehand
The President has no power at all to sign any bill into law

questions.prompt: Which level of government usually sets driver license rules?
choices: A school district
Each state government
The federal government alone
The United Nations

questions.prompt: What does the Supremacy Clause say about conflicts?
choices: Valid federal law wins over a conflicting state law
City law always wins over all state and federal law
The oldest law wins no matter which level made it
State law always wins over federal law within that state

questions.prompt: Mia moves from one state to another and finds that the minimum age for working in certain jobs is different. What best explains this?
choices: Only the United Nations can set rules about work for young people
One of the states must be breaking the Constitution
Work rules are always decided by each school principal
States may set many rules themselves, so laws can vary by place

questions.prompt: A city passes an ordinance. It conflicts with a valid state law on the same subject. Which statement is most accurate in general?
choices: The ordinance wins since cities know their own local needs best
Both apply equally and the person may choose which one to follow
The ordinance may be invalid since valid state law can override it
The federal government must automatically take over the whole dispute

questions.prompt: In a civil case, who is the person who files the lawsuit?
choices: The plaintiff
The juror
The bailiff
The prosecutor

questions.prompt: Which standard of proof is used in a criminal trial?
choices: A hint of suspicion
Beyond a reasonable doubt
More likely than not
Probably true

questions.prompt: A store employee is hurt when a shelf falls. She sues the store for her medical bills. What kind of case is this?
choices: A juvenile case, which is only for people under age eighteen
A constitutional case, which only the Supreme Court is able to hear
A civil case, usually seeking money or a court order
A criminal case, where the government always seeks jail time

questions.prompt: A driver is found not guilty in a criminal trial for causing a crash. The injured pedestrian later wins a civil case against the driver. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The judge in the civil case was allowed to ignore all of the evidence
The pedestrian had to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt again there
The civil verdict is invalid since it contradicts the criminal one
The civil case used a lower standard of proof than the criminal case

questions.prompt: In a jury trial, what is the main job of the jury?
choices: To write the laws that apply to the case
To act as the lawyer for the defendant
To keep order and control the courtroom
To decide what the facts are and reach a verdict

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a defendant is presumed innocent?
choices: The defendant may not be questioned by any lawyer at trial
The defendant need not attend the trial at all if unwilling
The government must prove guilt, and the defendant need not disprove it
The judge has already decided that the defendant did nothing

questions.prompt: In a bench trial, who decides the facts and the verdict?
choices: A randomly chosen witness
The judge
The defendant's family
The prosecutor

questions.prompt: A defendant cannot afford a lawyer and is charged with a serious crime. Which constitutional idea best explains why the court appoints one?
choices: Due process and the right to counsel, which protect fair trials
The Supremacy Clause, which makes federal law outrank state law
The veto power, which lets officials stop unfair prosecutions
The right to trial by jury, which includes choosing the jurors

questions.prompt: What is the main original idea behind having a separate juvenile justice system?
choices: Young people should always get harsher punishments than adults do
Young people should never be held responsible for anything
Young people can change, so guidance and rehabilitation matter
Young people may not have lawyers or any other legal rights

questions.prompt: What did In re Gault (1967) say about young people in delinquency cases that could lead to loss of freedom?
choices: They can be questioned freely without any notice of charges
They have no due process rights since the court is informal
They must always be tried in adult court with a jury
They have important due process rights such as the right to a lawyer

questions.prompt: A state hearing says a teen was "adjudicated delinquent" and orders probation and community service. What does this show about juvenile court?
choices: The language and results differ from adult criminal court
The case must be heard on television for the public
The teen cannot appeal or have any legal representation
The result is called a conviction and always means prison

questions.prompt: Two people debate whether some serious juvenile cases should be moved to adult court. One cites public safety. The other cites young people's ability to change. What is the best description of this disagreement?
choices: A disagreement about the meaning of a treaty between two nations
A policy debate where states make choices within constitutional limits
A dispute only about facts that a jury can settle once and for all
A question that the Constitution answers with one clear rule for every state

questions.prompt: Which amendment is the source of the right to remain silent?
choices: The Tenth Amendment
The Fifth Amendment
The First Amendment
The Second Amendment

questions.prompt: According to Miranda v. Arizona (1966), when must police give the warnings?
choices: Before questioning a person who is in custody
Any time police speak to anyone for any reason at all
